cl_mdma_feelings.short: Mostly good: in lab studies, 67 in 100 called it positive afterwards. It lasted about four hours. Many also got a dry mouth or a clenched jaw.
cl_mdma_feelings.but: These were healthy volunteers in a lab, given a known pill and nothing else. The one club study was small, with no dummy pill.
how: In Basel labs, 136 healthy adults rated the good feeling about 80 out of 100, against 3 or 4 on a dummy pill. In a study of 32, people felt more open and closer to others.
Unwanted effects came too: 55 in 100 had a dry mouth and 40 in 100 of those asked clenched their jaw. Looking back, 67 in 100 called it positive, 15 in 100 disappointing or bad.
It began in about half an hour on average and lasted about four hours. For some the start was slow; an antidepressant given first cut the effect. Nobody took more, so that wasn't tested.
At a London club, people who took ecstasy weren't clearly happier than other clubbers. Two days later they felt sadder, but not a week later. Pills were untested, so MDMA's part is unclear.
cl_mdma_feelings.rate: Lab trials where each volunteer got both MDMA and a dummy pill, and the gap was huge; one step below strong for possible bias. The club study alone would rate very low.
cl_mdma_feelings.note: Short answers first with 67 in 100; added closeness finding; dropped unblinding remark, which the claim lacks.

cl_gen_release_deaths.short: Yes. In the first week out, the risk of dying was about 1.5 to 2 times that of later weeks. Drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause.
cl_gen_release_deaths.but: It's death records only: they don't name the drugs, and nobody measured tolerance, so the study can't say why.
how: Researchers used death records for about 1.5 million people who left prison or jail in eight countries, between 1980 and 2018.
16 of the 18 groups had records for each day. In them, the risk of dying in days 2 to 7 after release was about 1.5 to 2 times the risk in later weeks.
Drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause, in that first week and overall. Yet 91 in 100 of those deaths came after week 4, since people were followed for much longer than that.
The study had no information on drug use, treatment or tolerance. So it cannot say why the first week is riskier.
cl_gen_release_deaths.rate: Death records of 1,471,526 people released from prison or jail in eight countries, all analysed the same way. But it is one study, and how causes were recorded wasn't checked.
cl_gen_release_deaths.note: Short now says yes first; explained the 91-in-100 puzzle; But says plainly why remains unknown.

cl_opi_using_alone.short: Very common: 76 in 100 people at harm reduction sites had used alone at least once in the past week. The top reason: it's easier and more comfortable at home.
cl_opi_using_alone.but: It was one survey in one part of Canada. Everyone asked already went to these sites.
how: In 2018, 414 people at 27 sites in British Columbia, Canada, did a short survey. The sites hand out safer-use supplies.
Of those who used alone, 44 in 100 said using at home was easier and more comfortable; 14 in 100 did not want others to know. Some wrote that they had no one to use with.
People who used alone more often had no steady home: 38 in 100, against 24 in 100 of those who didn't.
The survey could not show if using alone changes overdose risk. It cites coroners' reports. They found that about 7 in 10 people who died of an overdose there in 2016 and 2017 were using alone.
cl_opi_using_alone.rate: One survey of 414 people who happened to visit harm reduction sites in British Columbia in 2018. Nobody told them what counted as alone, and reasons were picked from a short list.

freq.what: had used drugs alone at least once in the past week
freq.note: 314 of 414 people at 27 harm reduction sites in British Columbia, Canada, in 2018.

cl_opi_using_alone.note: Short opens very common with 76 in 100, matching the picture; added housing numbers; rate drops quote marks.

cl_xc_music.q: Does music change how a trip goes?
cl_xc_music.short: Nobody knows for sure: no study we read compared music with silence. 18 of 19 patients said music helped at times; 10 said it sometimes made things harder.
cl_xc_music.but: The one test that compared two playlists had just 10 people, so it could easily miss a difference.
how: 19 patients with hard-to-treat depression took psilocybin in a clinic with music. Almost all said it helped at times; about half said it sometimes made things harder.
Patients who spoke more warmly about the music had a bigger drop in depression a week later. But both were measured at the same time.

In a trial of 10 people trying to quit smoking, each had one session with classical music and one with gongs and singing bowls, in random order. How mystical or hard the sessions felt did not clearly differ.
In a US survey, people who linked their hardest time to the music did not rate it as harder than others did.
cl_xc_music.rate: One small trial of 10 people compared two playlists, not music with silence, and everyone knew which music played. The rest is what people said afterwards.
cl_xc_music.note: Short opens with nobody knows plus patients' counts; But names the tiny playlist test; question says trip.

cl_xc_difficult_how_common.q: How common are bad trips, and can problems last?
cl_xc_difficult_how_common.short: Fairly common: 41 in 100 people who'd used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip. 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life.
cl_xc_difficult_how_common.but: That's one online survey, and people were looking back over their whole lives.
how: 613 US adults who had ever used a psychedelic answered one online survey in 2021, looking back over their whole life.
Most were glad they had used psychedelics: 79 in 100 agreed, at least a little.
In the days or weeks after their hardest trip, 7 in 100 had thoughts of hurting themselves or others, or tried to.
57 in 100 said a problem like worry or poor sleep lasted at least a few days, and put it down to psychedelics. But nobody who hadn't used them was asked.
cl_xc_difficult_how_common.rate: One online survey of 613 US adults from a sign-up panel, matched only on sex, age and ethnicity. Two of its questions gave counts that don't agree, and no one who hadn't used psychedelics was asked.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people who had ever used a psychedelic, in one US online survey:
pairs: said they had had at least one difficult experience
said one had severely affected their ability to get through daily life
sought medical or psychological help afterwards
freq.note: 613 US adults asked once, in 2021, looking back over their whole life (251, 28 and 16 people). No one who had not used psychedelics was asked.

cl_xc_difficult_how_common.note: Short opens fairly common; question in people's words; rate no longer calls the clashing questions borrowed.

cl_gen_portugal.short: Mixed. Adults who'd ever tried a drug went from 8 to 12 in 100, but use in the last year barely moved. New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell.
cl_gen_portugal.but: Treatment and other help grew too, starting in 1999, so these figures can't show what the law alone did.
how: In 2001, having any drug for your own use became an offence handled by regional panels, not a crime. Mostly for that reason, crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to 5,000–5,500 a year.
Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100 (2001 to 2007); past-year use barely changed.
New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell from 907 (2000) to 267 (2008). The paper says this has been credited mainly to more harm reduction services, without saying by whom.
Deaths doctors judged drug-caused fell from about 76 to 20 (2001 to 2008). Deaths with drugs found fell, then rose as testing more than doubled.
cl_gen_portugal.rate: National figures before and after the law, loosely set beside Spain and Italy; treatment grew at the same time, and some counts changed method. The figures point both ways; both sides are below.

freq.what: adults (aged 15 to 64) in Portugal said in 2007 that they had ever used an illegal drug
freq.note: National surveys: 7.8 in 100 in 2001 (7.6 in the paper's table) and 12.0 in 2007. Use in the past year: 3.4 and 3.7 in 100.

cl_gen_portugal.note: Short opens Mixed with the picture's numbers; what the law did now leads How; rate cut to two sentences.

cl_dc_home_vs_service.q: Do take-home fentanyl strips match what trained staff find?
cl_dc_home_vs_service.short: For opioids, about the same. For meth and cocaine, take-home strips showed fentanyl far more often: 28 in 100 meth samples, against 5 in 100 tested by staff.
cl_dc_home_vs_service.but: The two groups tested different samples, and no lab checked which results were right.
how: In 2019, people took strips from ten health sites and used them at home a little over half the time. Staff tested other samples at the sites.
Opioids: 90 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, and 89 in 100 on site.
Crystal meth: 28 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, against 5 in 100 on site; cocaine, 17 against 1. The authors think most extra positives were false, but didn't test it.
People told the study their own results, often from memory.
cl_dc_home_vs_service.rate: One study in British Columbia in 2019 compared results people noted themselves with staff results on different samples. Nobody knows how many kits never came back, and many results were recalled later.

freq.title: Out of every 100 crystal meth samples, how many showed fentanyl?
pairs: tested by the person with a take-home strip
tested on site by trained staff
freq.note: 73 of 265 and 5 of 97 samples, British Columbia, 2019. Different samples; no lab checked which results were right.

cl_dc_home_vs_service.note: Added the 28-in-100 count; false-positive idea marked untested; dropped sheet-choice remark the claim lacks; question names fentanyl.

cl_meth_mechanism_release.short: It makes nerve cells let out three brain chemicals: dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin.
cl_meth_mechanism_release.but: How it does this is not fully known. So far we have only read a review about it.
how: Meth makes nerve endings let out dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin.
It seems to push them out of their storage sacs and run their pumps in reverse.
The details are not fully known. This comes from a review; we have not read the lab studies yet.
cl_meth_mechanism_release.rate: Lab and animal studies, known only through one review; the original studies haven't been read yet, so how good they are is unknown.
cl_meth_mechanism_release.note: Already plain and direct; copied unchanged.

cl_mdma_regulatory_2024.short: No. The US regulator turned it down in August 2024, after its expert panel voted 9 to 2 that the data didn't show it works.
cl_mdma_regulatory_2024.but: We read the panel's notes, but not the final letter.
how: In June 2024, the regulator's expert panel voted 9 to 2 that the data didn't show the treatment works, and 10 to 1 that the benefits didn't outweigh the risks.
Panel members worried that people could tell which pill they'd had. In one trial, 94 in 100 on MDMA and 75 in 100 on the dummy pill guessed right.
They also doubted the later check of whether benefits lasted, and noted that no study separated the drug's effect from the therapy's.
The regulator's own staff said the main trials had no lab tests on treatment days, and the company didn't log euphoria as a side effect, so misuse risk was harder to judge.
cl_mdma_regulatory_2024.rate: The panel's votes come from the regulator's own documents, but the final decision letter was not read, so the decision and its reasons are known mainly from news reports.
cl_mdma_regulatory_2024.note: Short answers No first with the 9-to-2 vote; added guess rates and euphoria logging from staff review.

cl_psi_smoking.short: Not known. In one small study, 12 of 15 people given psilocybin plus lots of counselling weren't smoking 6 months later.
cl_psi_smoking.but: There was no comparison group, so no one can tell what psilocybin added to all the counselling.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 15 adults who had smoked for 31 years on average got 15 weeks of counselling and psilocybin two or three times.
Six months on, breath and urine tests confirmed 12 of 15 given psilocybin weren't smoking. Four of those 12 had smoked again at some point.
The psilocybin paper cites 45 to 59 in 100 not smoking after intensive standard treatment. With so few people, 12 of 15 isn't clearly better.
cl_psi_smoking.rate: One small study: just 15 volunteers, all given psilocybin and lots of counselling, with no comparison group, so nobody can tell what psilocybin itself did.
cl_psi_smoking.note: Already answers first in plain words; copied unchanged.

cl_gen_deaths_news_stigma.short: Yes, somewhat. Readers judged the person who died more harshly when the story said heroin, not ecstasy, or an older person with years of use.
cl_gen_deaths_news_stigma.but: Readers saw one made-up story and answered straight away; nobody checked what they did later.
how: In 2022, 1,248 adults in the UK each read one made-up news story about a drug death, with the details chosen at random.
Readers judged the person more harshly when the person was a man, was older and had used the drug for years, or had taken heroin rather than ecstasy. The differences were small to moderate.
Support for services that reduce harm, such as drug checking, barely changed.
The study could not tell the effect of age apart from the effect of using the drug for longer.
cl_gen_deaths_news_stigma.rate: One online experiment in which chance decided which version of a made-up news story 1,248 UK adults read. The plan was not published first, and the stigma questions were new.
cl_gen_deaths_news_stigma.note: Short now answers yes, somewhat, first instead of opening with the study.

cl_coc_crack_powder.short: Possibly, though it's the same drug. People new to crack reported each sign of dependence more often: about 18 to 32 in 100, against 5 to 12 for powder.
cl_coc_crack_powder.but: Each person was asked once, so the surveys cannot show that crack itself is the reason.
how: Powder can't be smoked; crack is. A 1996 review links most differences to how each is taken, how fast and how much cocaine that delivers, and how much people use, not the form itself.
In US surveys from 1995 to 1998, about 18 to 32 in 100 people who had just started crack reported each sign of dependence. For people who had just started powder, it was 5 to 12 in 100.
After allowing for how many days people had used, and for age, drinking, smoking and injecting, the gap was smaller but did not go away.
A review of 302 studies found comparisons of crack with other cocaine mixed. Its authors say crack is not a likely direct cause of the infections and violence linked to it.
cl_coc_crack_powder.rate: US household surveys from 1995–1998 that asked people once, with no way to know how people differed before they started. A review of 302 articles says the wider research disagrees.
cl_coc_crack_powder.note: Short answers possibly with dependence counts; How point 1 drops route timing, keeps the review's same-drug explanation.

cl_meth_dependence_baserate.q: How many people who use stimulants like meth get hooked?
cl_meth_dependence_baserate.short: It depends how you count. An old US survey found 11 in 100 had ever been dependent; a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting.
cl_meth_dependence_baserate.but: Neither survey has a number for meth alone, and the two measured different things, so they can't be compared directly.
how: In the early 1990s, a US survey used set interview questions to find who had ever been dependent on a drug they had used.
Stimulants other than cocaine: about 11 in 100. Tobacco 32, alcohol 15, cocaine 17.
It counted people who had just started, so they had little time to become dependent.
An Australian survey in 2007 counted differently, allowing for when people started. It estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting, but it also counted a related diagnosis called abuse.
cl_meth_dependence_baserate.rate: Two household surveys, in the US in 1990 to 1992 and Australia in 2007. The US one lumped meth with other stimulants, prescription pills included, and the Australian one never said which stimulants.

freq.what: of people who had used stimulants other than cocaine had been dependent at some point
freq.note: US survey, 1990 to 1992: stimulants other than cocaine, not meth alone. Tobacco was measured differently.
freq.compare_k: For comparison, in the same survey:

cl_meth_dependence_baserate.note: Short opens it depends with both figures; question says hooked; Australian method explained, quote marks dropped.

cl_mdma_nonlinear.q: Does taking more MDMA raise blood levels more than you'd expect?
cl_mdma_nonlinear.short: Yes, it seems so: a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.8 times higher, and about twice the total over the day.
cl_mdma_nonlinear.but: Only 8 men were compared, in a lab, and the study was not planned to look at this.
how: In 8 men, a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.8 times higher and about twice the total over the day.
The kidneys cleared MDMA at the same pace at both doses; the rest of the body cleared it about half as fast at the larger one.
The authors suggest the breakdown gets saturated or that MDMA blocks the enzyme that clears it. They also say people may be more prone to acute toxicity; toxicity was not measured.

People can feel little from an amount for several reasons: a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts it, or bodies that differ. Some take more. These studies didn't test that.
cl_mdma_nonlinear.rate: One lab trial in which each of 8 men was his own comparison. Blood was tested directly, but this analysis was added afterwards, and with so few men the extra rise could be chance.
cl_mdma_nonlinear.note: Short says yes first; question asks whether, not why; removed liver, absent from claim; trimmed felt-little point.
